doc.title: Larry Ridley interviewed by Monk Rowe, Toronto, Canada, January 10, 2003

title: Schomburg residency and the African-American Jazz Caucus
summary: His artist-in-residence work at the Schomburg Center and Jazz Caucus efforts to restore jazz at historically black colleges.

story.theme_name: Late-career reflections: awards, legacy and life lessons
story.community_name: Looking back: no regrets, what it all meant

blocks.x: been jazz artist in residence at the Schomburg Center which is a part of the New York Public Library.
Sure. I visited there one time when they were doing a photo opening or something.

Right. And I play in jazz artists in residence there. I do three concerts a year and I’m working at doing interviews similar to what we’re doing here, and also developing workshops to have a young junior scholars program that they have instituted that’s being funded by New York Life, and we’re working to bring young people to understand a variety of things that they can look at as far as career paths are concerned. So I’m trying to be very active and then I’m with the executive director of the African-American Jazz Caucus and I took over that in the past couple of years and spent a lot of my own personal money and a lot of my personal time in doing a lot of this stuff myself. And I brought to fruition a project that I’d been wanting to see at the IAJE conference, an all- star student jazz ensemble comprised of students from the historically black colleges and universities. And our primary mission is that we’re trying to develop the programs that the HBC used because they were originators of jazz education. Because it was the Jubilee Singers and the jazz bands that were the prime money makers for these institutions early on. It was only after the NFL and the marching bands became the predominant thing, because they were the — the Gramblings and the Florida A&Ms, they were doing all the halftime events at the NFL so it became a revenue stream. So at the historical black colleges and universities, the marching band became the heavy focus in many of them. And we’re working to change that emphasis so that it’s not just that but that the jazz and even the blues and other spiritual and so on, and people have to understand that the Gospels grew out of the spirituals. The spirituals were first. And the inner city schools. We’ve got kids coming up that don’t, you know the quality of education that they’re getting is horrendous. The lack of substance that they are receiving is just incredible. So we’ve got a big job cut out for us and it’s taking everybody — I mean and the African- American Jazz Caucus is not just a closed society of only African-Americans. We’re looking at anybody who recognizes what our mission is about and is empathetic with what we’re trying — because we’re not just talking about this for the benefit of just African-Americans. We’re talking about making reality about what the history has been. Because history has been so totally distorted in many cases that we need to go back. If we’re talking about revisionism, which we know is going on, we need to make sure that we revise it correctly and with substance and not cliché metaphors and all this other kind of glib Johnny-come-lately nonsense that some people entertain.
Well we need more people around here like yourself.
And I congratulate you on your career and what you’re doing now. It’s fantastic. © Fillius Jazz Archive -23-
